entries.title: Nigeria: Suspected oil thieves dead after inhaling fumes
entries.summary: A Nigerian environmental group says that at least 37 people died trying to siphon crude oil off a ship illegally. Police acknowledged a fatal incident but gave fewer details, saying investigations continued.
entries.content:
September 4, 2026

A Nigerian environmental group says that at least 37 people died trying to siphon crude oil off a ship illegally. Police acknowledged a fatal incident but gave fewer details, saying investigations continued.

A Nigerian environmental NGO says that at least 37 people died in an attempt to tap oil from a loading vessel in the south of the country illegally. 

Most of them died as a result of inhaling hazardous fumes, the Youth and Advocacy Centre said.

Nigerian authorities were yet to issue a death toll but had acknowledged a fatal incident in which people were killed, apparently while trying to steal crude oil. 

What do we know about the case?

The incident took place overnight on Thursday in Okrika in Rivers State in the oil-rich Niger Delta in the south of the country. 

The environmental group said it happened at a jetty as a vessel was loading oil from the Indorama Eleme Petrochemical through the Port Harcourt Refinery. The people who died were "suspected oil thieves" trying to siphon the commodity off into boats at an "illegal tapping point."

The Youth and Advocacy Centre NGO said that other people were still missing, potentially lost in the water, quoting a network of volunteers.

Police acknowledged an incident but said they continued to investigate the details.

"The Rivers State Police Command can confirm the deaths. The victims were allegedly attempting to steal crude oil," said spokesperson Blessing Agbabe.

Oil theft is fairly common in the Niger Delta region of Nigeria, Africa's biggest oil producer, with oil mining areas hotspots for poverty and environmental degradation.

The Nigerian government estimates that oil theft causes losses worth several billion dollars annually and has been trying to clamp down on the practice.

The tapping process can also cause leaks and environmental damage.

If confirmed this would be the worst fatal accident on record connected to attempted oil theft since at least October 2023.

However the Nigeria Security and Civil Defense Corps said that the casualty figures circulating remained unverified, saying it was working with other security agencies to clarify the details.

entries.title: Germany, partners aim to finalize 'return hubs' by year end
entries.summary: German Interior Minister Dobrindt said "technical discussions" were underway with non-EU countries to establish controversial "return hubs." Rights organizations have questioned the legality and morality of the plans.
entries.content:
September 4, 2026

German Interior Minister Dobrindt said "technical discussions" were underway with non-EU countries to establish controversial "return hubs." Rights organizations have questioned the legality and morality of the plans.

Germany and other European Union countries are aiming to finalize so-called "return hubs," detention centers outside the bloc where they wish to send migrants whose asylum requests have been rejected, by the end of the year.

The European Parliament in June approved tougher migration rules that paved the way for the creation of "return hubs."

"We want to reach an agreement with third countries this year," which would then enable the establishment of so-called "return hubs," said German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt after a meeting with his counterparts from Denmark, Greece, Austria and the Netherlands in Copenhagen on Friday.

He added that "technical discussions" were currently underway with countries outside the EU, but did not name such countries.

What did the EU ministers say on 'return hubs?'

The five EU countries whose ministers attended the Copenhagen meeting are seeking a deal with an undisclosed non-EU country to host the "return hubs."

Uganda and Rwanda in particular are seen as possibilities —two autocratically ruled countries.

"Around New Year, we expect to have a common understanding with a partner country outside of the European Union," said Danish Migrations Minister Morten Bodskov.

Both the Greek and Danish migration ministers said they wished for the "return hubs" to become operational by 2027.

"We do not accept that foreigners staying illegally in Denmark should be rewarded because of our difficulties in returning them," Bodskov said in an earlier statement.

The controversial scheme had already been briefly adopted by the United Kingdom under the former conservative government, but has since been scrapped after the social democratic Labour Party came to power.

In Italy, the right-wing government of Giorgia Meloni reached a similar deal with Albania which currently faces legal challenges.

Are EU 'return hubs' legal?

The legality of the plans for the so-called "return hubs" remains unclear under EU law.

A legal appraisal issued by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) in April concluded that the controversial Italian deportation centers in Albania do not violate European law.

EU law does not in principle prohibit member states from establishing such centers outside their own territory.

However, it stipulates that deportees continue to receive legal counsel and linguistic support, and are able to maintain contact with their families and the relevant authorities.

Andreas Grünewald, a migration expert with the German evangelical charity Brot für die Welt (Bread for the World), questioned the feasibility of the plans, calling them "practically difficult to implement and highly problematic in terms of human rights."

He said ministers risked running into "political dead ends."

Rights organizations criticize EU 'return hubs'

The highly controversial plan has been met with wide rejection from rights groups, including children's charities and church organizations, who have criticized the plans for what they see as the "criminalization of migration."

Marta Welander from the International Rescue Committee (IRC), a global humanitarian aid, relief and development NGO, said the plans risk "normalizing detainment in prison-like facilities" and warned that deportees may face "persecution, torture or worse" in their destination countries.

Caritas, a Catholic charity operating in Germany, Austria, Switzerland and Slovakia, said that migrants risked becoming trapped in a "legal grey area" if "arbitrarily and indefinitely detained" in the hubs.

Florian Westphal, CEO of Save The Children Germany, warned of the risks faced in particular by children and young people.

"The planned return centers in third countries are places of uncertainty and carry the risk of massive violations of children's rights," he said.

"Transferring children to states with which they have no connection, and where they face the risk of deprivation of liberty and are cut off from key figures in their lives, cannot be in their best interests. Children deserve unconditional protection, no matter where they come from or where they live."

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Nepal flood disaster puts climate justice under spotlight
entries.summary: The devastating Himalayan glacial floods have raised broader questions about who should bear the costs and responsibility for the impacts of climate-related disasters.
entries.content:
Nepal

Nepal flood disaster puts climate justice under spotlight

September 4, 2026

The devastating Himalayan glacial floods have raised broader questions about who should bear the costs and responsibility for the impacts of climate-related disasters.

Days after devastating floods swept through Nepal's Bhotekoshi-Trisuli river basin, the true scale of the disaster is still emerging.  

More than 1,250 people have been confirmed dead and almost 4,000 are still missing.

Buildings, bridges, roads and over a dozen hydropower facilities have been destroyed, causing an estimated $2.6 billion (€2.24 billion) in damage to public and private infrastructure, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).

Search and rescue operations for missing people remain underway, with families still hoping for their safe return.

The exact cause of the glacial collapse remains unclear, but experts say climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.

A global responsibility?

For Nepal, the disaster has raised a question that goes beyond rescue and reconstruction.

It's about climate justice and who should bear the costs and responsibility for such environmental disasters when the Himalayan nation contributes only a tiny fraction of global greenhouse gas emissions yet faces increasingly severe climate-related risks.

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said responding to the catastrophe is a "global responsibility."

"As we work tirelessly to address the damage caused by this sudden and massive disaster, a deeper question has also emerged: How did this destruction happen to us?" Shah asked while addressing Parliament this week.

"Mitigating and managing its impacts is regarded as a shared responsibility of the international community," he stressed.

Kathmandu is planning to raise climate justice issues in the upcoming United Nations General Assembly session in New York, where Prime Minister Shah himself is likely to lead the Nepali delegation.

"We will make our case about the impact of climate change and seek global support and moral obligation to tackle it," Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told DW. "We will also take the initiative of building a coalition of climate-vulnerable countries to raise our collective concerns."

Highly vulnerable to climate impacts

Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people, has contributed little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming.

The country accounts for just 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions and emits about 0.5 tons of CO₂ per person each year, making it a "negligible contributor to climate change," according to the World Bank.

But the landlocked Himalayan nation is highly vulnerable to the effects of climate change, with flooding, landslides, glacier-related hazards and other environmental risks threatening lives and livelihoods.

Nepal's leaders say the country needs long-term international support to adapt to a rapidly changing mountain environment.

The country's government estimates that implementing adaptation priorities between 2025 and 2035 could require as much as $18 billion to $20 billion. And Kathmandu wants international climate finance to provide most of these funds.

Nepal has spent years arguing in global climate forums that vulnerable mountain countries need greater support for adaptation and resilience.

In December 2009, Nepal held a historic Cabinet meeting at Kala Patthar, near Mount Everest base camp, at an altitude of 17,192 feet, to highlight the threats that climate change and glacial melting pose to Nepal and other mountainous nations.

Bimala Rai Paudyal, a former Nepali foreign minister, said the latest disaster meant "this is an opportune time for us to highlight glacier melting and climate justice issues in international climate forums."

"Earlier, we were advocating only about climate impacts. Now, we are heavily suffering from it," she told DW.

Paudyal believes Nepal is well positioned to lead an alliance of vulnerable countries, given its exposure to climate risk as well as its expertise and contribution to the climate justice efforts.

An opportunity for global climate action?

Kathmandu has formally approached the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)-backed "Loss and Damage Fund" for assistance over the latest floods.

But the fund, set up by the UN in 2025 to aid the impacts of climate change, has not yet begun distributing its limited cash.

The fund also relies on voluntary contributions and lacks legally binding commitments under current international climate agreements, leaving major emitters such as China, India and the US under no direct obligation to compensate for climate change impacts.

Still, some observers and climate advocates believe Nepal can present a strong case for urgent global climate action.

"Nepal can turn this tragedy into an opportunity for global climate action," Dinesh Paudel, professor of sustainable development at Appalachian State University in North Carolina, told DW. "For which, Nepal needs to build a consensus among national stakeholders and maneuver cautiously, considering geopolitical factors."

According to him, Kathmandu can create an ethical movement for climate justice by highlighting the recent flood. This could then lead to creating an effective and legally binding mechanism to deal with climate impacts in the future.

Ashok Swain, professor of peace and conflict research at Uppsala University and also UNESCO Chair on International Water Cooperation, shares a similar view.

"Nepal should not be left to pay for a climate crisis it did little to create or for regional non-cooperation over which it has limited influence," he said. "This is not a question of charity. It is fundamentally a question of climate justice and a fair distribution of responsibility."

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: How can African retailers compete with Shein and Temu?
entries.summary: Shein and Temu are expanding across Africa with low prices and vast product ranges. Businesses and unions warn the growth could come at a cost for local jobs.
entries.content:
September 4, 2026

Shein and Temu are expanding across Africa with low prices and vast product ranges. Businesses and unions warn the growth could come at a cost for local jobs.

A T-shirt for a few dollars, along with jewelry, shoes and accessories — all delivered straight to your door. For many young people in African cities, shopping no longer starts in a store.

They scroll through Instagram or TikTok, see influencers showing off their latest purchases, and place an order with just a few clicks.

This combination of extremely low prices, a huge selection and aggressive social media marketing has made Chinese company Shein one of the world's most successful online fashion retailers.

Temu, also from China, follows a similar model with an even broader range of products.

For Africa's young, urban consumers, the appeal is obvious. But as more purchasing power flows directly to Asia through these platforms, another question is becoming increasingly important: What happens to local retailers, manufacturers and jobs?

South Africa shows the impact

South Africa is currently the clearest test case. Shein launched there in 2020, followed by Temu in 2024.

According to a study commissioned by the Localization Support Fund, the two platforms generated around 7.3 billion rand (about $405 million) in 2024. That represents 3.6% of the total market for clothing, textiles, footwear and leather, but already around 37% of online sales in the sector.

The study also estimates that 2,818 manufacturing jobs and 5,282 retail jobs failed to materialize during that period, a combined impact of about 8,100 jobs. By 2030, more than 34,000 additional retail and manufacturing jobs could be at risk under the study's modeled scenarios.

Simon Eppel, a research director with the South African Clothing and Textile Workers' Union (SACTWU), sees this as a growing threat to the domestic industry.

He says Shein and Temu have gained a significant market share in a short period of time and put local manufacturers under pressure.

"They sucked up billions of rands […] in sales, and undercut local manufacturers," Eppel said.

The union is calling for stricter controls.

"In fact, we propose to ban these apps in South Africa," added Eppel, noting that the SACTWU sees such a move as one possible measure to counter the effects of the price pressure.

Aggressive price competition

Industry experts have cautioned that online giants such as Shein can operate at a speed that is difficult for a small African retailer to match.

Digital data shows which products are in demand, while influencers, discounts and a constant stream of new offers encourage consumers to buy.

For users, the line between entertainment and shopping is becoming increasingly blurred. But price is a crucial factor for many consumers.

Tsonam Cleanse Akpeloo, chairman of the Association of Ghana Industries, Accra chapter (AGI Accra), stresses that the offers are particularly attractive in price-sensitive markets.

"Their prices are attractive in price-sensitive economies where consumers naturally look for products that fit their budgets," he told DW.

Local business owners say that problems arise when they can no longer compete on price.

Companies that rely on high-quality materials and higher standards are put at a competitive disadvantage.

In Ghana, Akpeloo has observed similar developments in sectors such as aluminum and hardware.

Nigeria: Cheap imports for urban youth

Nigeria is also an important market for the major Chinese online retailers. Temu has a dedicated platform for the market there, while Shein is building its reach primarily through influencers and fashion content.

The appeal is clear: a wide selection, low prices and access to international trends. But Nigeria has already experienced what cheap imports can do to a local industry.

For governments, therefore, the issue is not just fashion. It is also about the conditions under which local businesses can compete with global platforms.

Shein and Temu do not have a direct presence everywhere in Africa. Their strongest presence so far is in countries such as South Africa and Nigeria, and to some extent in Ghana and Kenya. But their products also reach customers indirectly in many other African countries.

So-called freight forwarders play an important role. They provide customers with a delivery address in a country where Shein or Temu delivers directly. The package is initially sent there and then forwarded to other places across Africa.

This is how it works for Mariama Sow from Guinea-Bissau. She orders shoes, accessories and human hair for hair salons from Shein. She uses a freight forwarder in Portugal, which then forwards her orders to Guinea-Bissau.

"Underwear, shoes, clothes and school supplies, and above all the human hair, live up to their promise," Sow said.

At the same time, she says she has heard complaints from other customers about poor quality or incorrect sizes. Another problem, she says, is that local retailers are losing customers, particularly younger ones.

The tax dispute shows the political dimension

For governments, the issue is also about taxes and fair competition. South Africa has therefore tightened the rules governing small online imports. The government wanted to prevent international platforms from enjoying a tax advantage over local retailers.

For a local retailer who pays rent, staff costs and taxes, such differences can be significant.

The conflict is therefore not simply a matter of China versus Africa. It is about whether local businesses can compete under comparable conditions.

Akpeloo from AGI Accra is also calling for better controls.

"We need stronger action against smuggling, better enforcement of customs and quality standards," he told DW.

Goods entering the market without the required duties and taxes can put additional pressure on local businesses.

Beyond cheap imports

Despite all the criticism, it would be too simplistic to portray the platforms solely as a threat.The key question is where the economic value is created.

A delivery driver earns money from an order placed in China. A textile worker, by contrast, can support an entire local value chain — from the fabric producer to the sewing factory and retailer.

For African governments, the challenge will therefore be to provide access to affordable products and digital commerce without weakening their own industrial base.

The real competition is no longer just between Shein, Temu and local retailers. It is also over the shopping habits of a young generation — and over whether Africa will remain primarily a consumer in the new digital economy or become a producer itself.

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: How vulnerable is Germany's infrastructure?
entries.summary: The growing number of attacks on substations and railway lines in Germany is raising concern. Experts say that people will have to get used to the likelihood that such incidents will continue.
entries.content:
Germany

How vulnerable is Germany's infrastructure?

September 4, 2026

The growing number of attacks on substations and railway lines in Germany is raising concern. Experts say that people will have to get used to the likelihood that such incidents will continue.

On Tuesday morning, unknown perpetrators attempted to attack the power supply near the coal-fired power plant at Jänschwalde in the eastern state of Brandenburg, partly succeeding in their objective. Then, later the same evening, a substation near Cologne suffered a disruption in what is believed to have been an act of sabotage.

On Wednesday, an explosion occurred near the railway station in the Bavarian city of Augsburg, caused by a hand grenade, according to investigators.

In the early hours of Thursday, several incendiary devices were thrown onto a construction site in Munich, close to a number of defense companies. Then, on Thursday evening, a suspicious object was discovered at a power substation in Dormagen, between Cologne and Düsseldorf. Investigators say a claim of responsibility has since been received.

While it remains entirely unclear who was behind the attacks in Jänschwalde, Cologne and Augsburg, investigators in Munich have arrested at least two suspects, reportedly Bulgarian nationals.

Already 160 attacks on critical infrastructure this year

What all these incidents have in common is that they appear to have targeted so-called critical infrastructure: energy facilities, the rail network, companies of strategic importance to national security and defense contractors.

Taken together, these sites can hardly be protected in their entirety. According to media reports citing an internal document, the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) has recorded 160 potential acts of sabotage and more than 700 suspicious drone sightings so far this year.

People in Berlin express concern over Russia

Even if the exact circumstances of each incident remain unclear, their rapid succession has created a growing sense of constant threat among the public. To find out how people are reacting, DW spoke to residents on the streets of Berlin.

One woman described her immediate reaction: "Fear. I was just talking about it with a colleague. It makes me feel very uneasy. I think about it a lot, and yet no one really talks about it. Maybe it's because people are afraid and would rather push it out of their minds?"

One man added: "We first need to recognize that something is happening, that we are under attack. I have very close ties to Russia and very close Russian friends, and it is very, very painful to see what is happening."

A freeze in German-Russian relations

The fact that Russia is the first thing that comes to many people's minds when they hear about the recent wave of attacks is hardly surprising. On Tuesday, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of Bavaria's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), both members of the governing alliance with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), appeared before the press. They announced that the German government is convinced Russian actors were behind the attempted drone attack on Halle/Leipzig Airport on August 4.

The government responded by closing Russia's consulate general in Bonn and ending the lease on the Russian House in Berlin. Moscow, in turn, retaliated by shutting down the Goethe-Institut in Moscow. Relations between Germany and Russia are now at their lowest point in years.

"We are no longer at peace, but neither are we at war," Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) remarked last year.

The reality is that since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in the spring of 2022, Germany has been among Ukraine's strongest supporters, both financially and militarily. That holds true even though successive German governments, including the current one, have consistently maintained that the country is not itself a party to the war.

Germany's support for Ukraine as a motive?

Since then, the Bundeswehr, after years of continuous downsizing, has undergone rapid rearmament, driven in part by concerns that Russia could pose a threat even to central Europe.

Neither at war nor at peace: Sönke Marahrens, a colonel in the German armed forces and a security expert at Kiel University, believes Germans would be well advised to prepare for this new form of confrontation, whoever may be responsible for it.

He told DW: "Hybrid warfare and hybrid activities are, in my view, essentially the same thing because they rely on the same methods. Foreign states or organizations pursue their strategic interests without resorting to diplomacy. This can take the form of sabotage, disinformation or attacks on critical infrastructure."

At the same time, the researcher stresses that it would be difficult to describe the situation as a state of war.

Private firms urged to strengthen infrastructure security

But it would be too simplistic to attribute every such incident immediately and unequivocally to Russia. Earlier this year, for example, an attack on a cable bridge in southwest Berlin caused a power outage that lasted several days. Hundreds of thousands of people were affected in freezing temperatures. In that case, which remains unsolved, suspicion has fallen on far-left extremists.

A debate has long been underway in Germany over how best to prepare for such attacks in the future. This spring, the government passed legislation known as "KRITIS," aimed at strengthening the protection of critical infrastructure, although the law has yet to enter into force.

Herbert Reul (CDU), the interior minister of the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, noted in an interview with public broadcaster ZDF that critical facilities, including those operated by private companies, can already be monitored through video surveillance. Responsibility for securing the surrounding areas, however, lies with authorities such as the police.

As Reul put it: "In Germany, we are sensitive when it comes to video surveillance and, more generally, to measures that affect civil liberties or data protection."

Reul argued that companies themselves need to invest more in protecting their facilities. The German Police Union (DPolG) takes a similar view. Its chairman, Heiko Teggatz, said that safeguarding critical infrastructure is not primarily the responsibility of the police, but first and foremost of the operators themselves.

"Those responsible for the security of their facilities must also invest in their protection," Teggatz said.

What is lacking, he argued, is not technical capability but a consistent willingness to invest.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Romania prosecutors indict Andrew Tate for trafficking minors
entries.summary: The social media influencer has also been indicted for money laundering and sex with a minor. His brother Tristan has been indicted for complicity.
entries.content:
September 4, 2026

The social media influencer has also been indicted for money laundering and sex with a minor. His brother Tristan has been indicted for complicity.

Prosecutors in Romania on Friday officially indicted social media influencer Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan on trafficking charges, years after investigation into the brothers' activities began.

Andrew Tate was indicted for trafficking minors, money laundering, sex with a minor and witness tampering. His brother has been indicted for complicity.

The brothers hold dual US and British citizenship.

They were arrested in Miami in late July, following a British request for their extradition on rape charges.

Andrew Tate is one of the most prominent faces of the "manosphere", a male-centered social media movement rooted in anti-feminist discourse. 

What did the Romanian prosecutors say about the Tates' indictment?

The Tate brothers have been mainly based in Romania since 2017, where they have been under criminal investigations since December 2022 on charges including human trafficking.

Romanian prosecutors said the Tates recruited their victims by falsely claiming to be seeking a relationship or marriage. They would then force them to produce pornographic content for a webcam business from which they mostly kept the profit.

The Romanian anti-organized crime prosecuting unit DIICOT said one of Andrew Tate's victims was only 15 when he seduced her in Britain in 2012, then moved her to Bucharest.

He then went on to exercise physical violence and mental intimidation to force her to produce pornographic content for social media sites.

Tristan was an accessory in the sexual exploitation committed by his brother, DIICOT said, using physical aggression to coerce the victim.

According to prosecutors, the Tates kept $1.25 million (roughly €1 million) from the camshow income generated by sexually exploiting the victim, which amounts to some 80% of her gains. They then tried to launder the funds by buying four luxury cars.

Can the Tates be extradited to Romania?

The spokesperson for DIICOT said it was not immediately clear whether the unit will seek the brothers' extradition from the US.

While they can be tried in absentia in Romania, the trial will not start immediately. Romanian laws stipulate that the indictment be sent to a preliminary court chamber for a judge to ensure the legality of the case files.

The preliminary chamber judge has 60 days to finalize the report, as per the law, but indictments tend to take significantly longer.

Andrew Tate, who is a self-proclaimed misogynist, and his brother have denied any wrongdoing.

"We ‌will examine every aspect of [the indictment] with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process," a Romanian lawyer for the Tates, Eugen Vidineac, said in a statement.

Edited by: Zac Crellin, Natalie Muller

entries.title: Majority of Germans see Russia as a threat
entries.summary: More than half of German citizens believe that Germany's security is threatened by Russia, according to the latest ARD Deutschlandtrend survey.
entries.content:
Germany

Majority of Germans see Russia as a threat

September 4, 2026

More than half of German citizens believe that Germany's security is threatened by Russia, according to the latest ARD Deutschlandtrend survey.

In the past few weeks, Germany has seen a drone attack on Leipzig Airport and an arson attack near defense contractors in Bavaria, while explosive devices and pyrotechnics were found at two substations in Brandenburg and North Rhine-Westphalia.

As the country enters a September featuring three vital state elections, attacks on critical infrastructure appear to be on the rise, and defense contractors are apparently in the crosshairs.

After some initial hesitation, the German government has now publicly blamed Russia for the Leipzig attack, but could the Kremlin also be behind the other attacks? "We are not at war, but we are no longer at peace either," said Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, of the Bavaria's conservatives, the Christian Social Union (CSU), has also warned that Germany has now become a "daily target of hybrid warfare," referring to measures that are not military, but are nonetheless meant to destabilize a country and unsettle the population — including cyberattacks, espionage, propaganda, disinformation, and acts of sabotage. 

The developments seem to have alarmed the German people. Some 56% of the eligible voters polled now see Germany's security as threatened by Russia, according to the latest Deutschlandtrend, for which the polling firm infratest-dimap conducted a representative survey of 1,319 German voters for public broadcaster ARD between August 31 and September 2.

East Germans are significantly less concerned

But not all Germans feel this way. Nearly half of citizens in eastern Germany, for instance, feel only slightly threatened, or not at all, by Russia. The same goes for supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), some of whose prominent figures have expressed support for Russia. The survey found that two-thirds of AfD supporters consider the threat from Russia to be low.

The same divisions in the German population emerge on the question of arms exports to Ukraine. Just over half of Germans consider the country's military support for Ukraine appropriate, or think it should even be expanded, but for just over four in ten Germans, that support goes too far. Opposition to sending weapons to Ukraine predominates in eastern Germany and among AfD supporters.

AfD holds steady lead nationwide

The eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt will elect a new state parliament on Sunday, and the AfD continues to be way ahead in the polls and could even win an absolute majority — usually unheard of in German elections. 

The party also continues to enjoy strong support at the national level. The new poll suggests that if a general election were held this coming Sunday, the AfD would receive 27% of the vote, one point less than in August, which would make it the largest party in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag. 

The CDU/CSU, meanwhile, remains in second place at 21%, well below the 28.5% it managed in the Bundestag election in February 2025. The Greens would receive 15%, while the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the socialist Left Party have seen slight improvements compared to August, reaching 13% and 12%, respectively (+1 each). All other parties would fail to clear the 5% threshold.

Unpopular government, unpopular chancellor

The latest poll also suggests that the current governing coalition of the CDU/CSU and the Social Democrats would no longer have a majority if an election were held now.

Only 15% of those surveyed are satisfied with the government's performance, and even among supporters of the governing parties themselves, a majority is disappointed with the incumbent coalition's performance. Chancellor and CDU leader Friedrich Merz fares even worse: Only 13% approve of his work.

This is consistent with how citizens assess the CDU/CSU's competence.

Also notable is that significantly fewer voters believe the CDU/CSU is capable of finding solutions in key policy areas. While just over a year ago, 31% still considered those parties competent to ensure peace in Europe, that figure has now dropped to just 23%.

A similar loss of confidence in the CDU/CSU is apparent elsewhere: On asylum and refugee policy, on pension reform, and on climate and environmental policy.

On the topic of the economy, the CDU/CSU still enjoys the highest level of public confidence at 24%, but here too, the figure has dropped significantly from 31% in February 2026.

In eastern Germany, the AfD is now the party in which citizens place the most confidence across all policy areas surveyed, with the exception of climate and environmental policy.

Economy causing concern

For many months now, Germans have viewed the economic situation as the most pressing problem to be solved. As many as 79% of respondents in the ARD Deutschlandtrend survey say the economy is doing poorly or very poorly. Here, too, however, there are significant differences depending on party affiliation.

As many as 41% of SPD supporters view the economic situation as good or very good, and 37% of Green Party supporters say the same. In contrast, only 3% of AfD supporters share this view — they are much more pessimistic, with 96% saying the economy is poor or very poor.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Two Reform UK officials resign amid donation breach reports
entries.summary: A Channel 4 report alleges that the party officials accepted foreign donations to fund three polls, illegal under the UK's electoral law. The allegations, which the party denies, come amid its annual conference.
entries.content:
United Kingdom

Two Reform UK officials resign amid donation breach reports

September 4, 2026

A Channel 4 report alleges that the party officials accepted foreign donations to fund three polls, illegal under the UK's electoral law. The allegations, which the party denies, come amid its annual conference.

Reform UK's annual conference on Friday is being overshadowed by a fresh scandal, after a Channel 4 report alleged that the populist party flouted electoral laws by accepting foreign donations.

Senior party officials James Orr and Dan Jukes have stepped down following the allegations, and the party said it was launching an internal investigation.

The hard-right Reform denies wrongdoing, with leader Nigel Farage saying nothing illegal took place.

The allegations come at a time when the party is struggling with a dip in popularity fueled by similar scandals as well as the replacement of former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer with Andy Burnham.

Farage is due to address the conference and was hoping his speech would restore some of his popularity. Jordan Bardella, the leader of France's anti-immigrant, eurosceptic National Rally (RN) party, is also due to address the conference on Friday.

What are the latest allegations against Reform UK?

The Channel 4 investigation alleges that the two senior Reform figures had arranged for a US company to pay over £30,000 (roughly €35,000 or $40,570) for three party-commissioned opinion polls.

British laws on political funding ban foreign donations.

According to the investigation, the donors were in fact undercover reporters from an independent organization founded by journalists from the Center for Climate Reporting, called Verbatim.

Orr, the party's head of policy, said that Reform had not been involved in commissioning the poll.

"There's absolutely no way this could amount to a benefit or donation in kind at all," he said, "It wasn't internal party polling. It wasn't Reform UK's poll. It was a public poll arranged by an independent person paying an independent pollster, and those polls ​were published immediately for the general public."

Farage, 62, insisted in an interview with LBC radio that Reform had "broken no laws" and was the victim of "entrapment."

Reform's popularity dips ahead of annual conference

The latest scandal has overshadowed the party's annual conference in Birmingham. But on the ground at the party conference, most activists don’t seem to be too bothered about the allegations.

Mary, a party member from London who did not want to give her surname, described it as a "storm in a teacup." She said she was there to learn about wider policies, and not paying attention to the donations.

Others believe that Reform is being scrutinized more than other parties.

"They are out to get them," said David McGrath from Folkestone on England‘s South Coast.

Together with his wife Susan, they have joined the party because they are concerned about migration. "The more money Reform receive, the better," the pair agreed.

Farage had also hoped to turn the tide on a popularity dip mainly fueled by another scandal.

The veteran Brexit campaigner faces a parliamentary watchdog probe over a £5 million donation from crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne in 2024 which he had failed to declare to parliamentary authorities.

Farage denies any wrongdoing, saying the sum was received before he was elected and was therefore not subject to declaration.

Still, the scandal has had an impact on Farage and his party's popularity, especially since the Labour party swapped leaders earlier in the summer, with Andy Burnham replacing Keir Starmer as the country's prime minister and in doing so, restoring some of the ruling party's popularity.

Farage is eyeing the top position after Reform managed to chalk up significant success at May local elections, prior to Starmer's departure.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Germany: Police suspect sabotage after another device found
entries.summary: A suspicious object that could damage power lines has been found near a German substation for a third time this week. DW has more.
entries.content:
Published September 4, 2026last updated September 4, 2026

A suspicious object that could damage power lines has been found near a German substation for a third time this week. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Police investigate after suspicious object found near Dormagen electricity substation
  • Saxony-Anhalt parties launch final campaign push ahead of Sunday vote
  • Volkswagen to shed 100,000 jobs by 2030

Welcome to our roundup of news and analysis from Germanyon Friday, September 4.

Tired of missing our real time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google. 

Skip next section Berlin: hackers publish stolen data after deadline expires

Berlin: hackers publish stolen data after deadline expires

A ransomware group which claimed to have stolen terabytes of sensitive data form government agencies in Berlin has carried out its threat to publish the data online.

The hackers ‌had ​previously demanded a ransom of 30 bitcoin (around €2 million or $2.3 million) for the data, but authorities ​in ​the German ​capital refused to submit to extortion.

A countdown on the hackers' leak website reached zero at 3:35 p.m. on Friday. An initial link led to an error page but, around one hour later, the 5.8-terabyte package was indeed made available.

IT experts have nevertheless praised the Berlin Senate's refusal to pay – which it would be legally unable to do anyway.

"If you continue to support these groups with money or in other ways, they'll just carry on," Bianca Kastl from Chaos Computer Club told local public broadcaster RBB. "You have to bleed them out financially."

The hacker group, which calls itself Rhysida, claimed to have acquired around 1.44 million files, including over 5,000 personal files and sensitive information on fines, pay checks, parliamentary committee meetings and even details on the vulnerabilities of Berlin's drinking water system.

Skip next section Half of VW's job cuts will be in Germany, Lower Saxony's state premier says

Half of VW's job cuts will be in Germany, Lower Saxony's state premier says

Nearly half of Volkswagen's 50,000 job cuts will be in Germany, with no agreement on plant closure, Lower Saxony's state Premier Olaf said on Friday

Lies is also a member of the group's supervisory board, .

The premier stressed that stopping car production in plants such as Emden or Hanover is unimaginable. He added that there was a chance to retain production at German plans by considering other perspectives.

"The day before yesterday, there was ​talk of closing the plants. With the decision [on the group's future], there ⁠is ​an opportunity to create prospects ​both in car manufacturing and, where that ​might not be ‌possible, through other ways," Lies said.

Late on Thursday, VW announced a major restructure that averted an escalation with unions and shareholders (see below.)

Skip next section July sees sharp jump in German factory orders

July sees sharp jump in German factory orders

German factory orders climbed in July for the third month in a row, according to official data from federal statistics office Destatis released on Friday,

Month-on-month industrial orders rose 2.5%, beating one expectation of just a 0.5% increase in a poll of analysts by the financial data platform FactSet.

The increase was mainly driven by an "exceptionally high volume" of large-scale orders for ships, railway rolling stock and aircraft, according to a Destatis press release. 

Industrial orders serve as an indicator of future business activity, and the recent increase is being interpreted by some analysts as a sign Germany's struggling economy is starting to recover. 

This week, the Ifo and RWI economic research institutes both sharply revised their 2026 GDP growth forecasts higher by 1.3 to 1.4%

"It has been a long while since such we have had such positive headlines about the German economy," LBBW bank analyst Jens-Oliver Niklasch told AFP news agency.

Factors including high energy prices, the rise of Chinese exports in competitive markets, and a faltering automotive sector have all weighed heavily on Germany's growth in recent years. 

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to borrow and spend hundreds of billions of euros in the coming years to boost industrial growth, mainly through defense and infrastructure.

Skip next section Hybrid attacks 'no coincidence' ahead of Sunday's state election — Interior Ministry

Hybrid attacks 'no coincidence' ahead of Sunday's state election — Interior Ministry

A German Interior Ministry spokesperson said it is "no coincidence" that several suspected acts of sabotage on electrical infrastructure have taken place this week, just days ahead of an important state election in Saxony-Anhalt.

"In the context of the ‌upcoming elections ... there is ‌an expectation that this may increase," the spokesperson said at a regular news conference.

Polling shows the election in the eastern German state on Sunday could see the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) come out on top, and potentially be able to govern a German state for the first timewith an outright majority. 

Police are investigating at least three suspected power grid sabotage attempts this week; two in North Rhine-Westphalia, and one in Brandenburg. Officials have not yet named suspects or a motive in any of the incidents. 

Skip next section Open electrical cabinet sparks police operation at Lower Saxony substation

Open electrical cabinet sparks police operation at Lower Saxony substation

Early Friday morning, a police patrol spotted an open cabinet at a power substation in the village of Ganderkesee, near Bremen in the northwestern state of Lower Saxony.

The find comes amid three suspected acts of sabotage at different substations in Germany over the past week. 

The officer who spotted the open cabinet called in additional personnel, a police spokesperson said Friday.

"Due to the special significance of the technical facility, the premises were immediately and thoroughly searched," the spokeswoman wrote.

No damage or unauthorized persons were found at the location.

"At no time was there any danger to the public," the spokesperson said.

Meanwhile, police near the western German city of Aachen are searching an area near a power plant in Weisweiler after receiving a letter from a man claiming responsibility for attempted sabotages elsewhere in Germany this week, and naming Weisweiler as a potential target.

Police have not said whether the man's claims are credible, nor whether any suspicious objects have been found during Friday morning's search.

Skip next section Germany's Zverev reaches third round of US Open

Germany's Zverev reaches third round of US Open

German tennis player Alexander Zverev came out on top after after a five-set clash with France's Quentin Halys at the US Open .

The four-hour 33-minute marathon at Arthur Ashe Stadium in New York City saw Zverev beat Halys 6-4, 4-6, 7-6 (3), 6-7 (3), 6-3.

The match was the second in a row for Zverev ending after 2 a.m. following a first-round five-setter against 89th-ranked Lorenzo Sonego on Wednesday.

After the second-round win, 2026 French Open winner Zverev said he wasn't happy with his performance, "but I won, that's the most important thing."

"I'm winning ugly right now. It's also a skill to win ugly and when you're not playing great tennis. I think I've mastered that right now," he said.

"Physically, I feel fine. I am proud, I think, to be physically quite strong. I just hope at some point I'll start playing better tennis," Zverev added.

His next match is set for Saturday against Chilean Alejandro Tabilo.

Skip next section Suspects in Munich arson attack to appear in court

Suspects in Munich arson attack to appear in court

The Bavarian State Criminal Police Office (LKA) on Friday said a 28-year-old woman and a 38-year-old man detained in connection with an arson attack in Munich are due to appear in court where a judge will decide whether to issue a formal arrest order.

Early Thursday morning, police were called to a fire at a construction site located near buildings in Munich's Berg am Laim neighborhood belonging to defense tech companies, including Helsing and Rohde & Schwarz.

Police said incendiary devices were thrown from a car. One was extinguished and did not cause any damage. Another was defused.

The suspects, both Bulgarian citizens, were arrested shortly after the incident at a nearby gas station. Police have not released any information about a possible motive.

Skip next section Volkswagen shares jump after 100,000 job cuts announced

Volkswagen shares jump after 100,000 job cuts announced

Markets on Friday responded positively after German automobile giant Volkswagen announced a major restructure that averted an escalation with unions and shareholder ​Lower ‌Saxony.

The carmaker announced on Thursday that it would be cutting a total of 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade in what is set to be the biggest restructuring ever seen in the global car industry.

The company said that management and trade unions had approved a plan involving the reduction of a further 50,000 jobs, in addition to 50,000 redundancies already agreed.

"It is essential to systematically align workforce levels with economic realities," read a statement from the multi-brand Volkswagen group which, apart from VW itself, also includes Audi and Porsche.

The total of 100,000 cuts amount to about 15% of Volkswagen staff worldwide. The cull eclipses the 50,000 job cuts General Motors made after it declared bankruptcy in 2009.

Unions and management had publicly rowed before signing off on the plans, with the former accusing the latter of not being honest with the workforce after the figure of 100,000 possible job cuts surfaced in the media before being communicated internally.

Volkswagen also said the long-term future of four major German plants – in Hannover, Emden, Zwickau and Neckarsulm — could not be guaranteed.

Their closure would mark the first full-scale shuttering of Volkswagen factories in its home country.

Skip next section Parties in Saxony-Anhalt hold final campaign events ahead of Sunday's polls

Parties in Saxony-Anhalt hold final campaign events ahead of Sunday's polls

The eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt goes to the polls on Sunday, and several parties are holding closing rallies on Friday to drum up support among undecided voters.

According to a survey by polling group "Forschungsgruppe Wahlen" cited by DPA news agency, 31% of respondents are still undecided.

Polls are showing the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in the lead as it aims for an a absolute majority that would allow it to lead a state government in Germany for the first time. 

The AfD's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund and national party chairman Tino Chrupalla are due at a campaign event in the state capital, Magdeburg.

Sven Schulze, currently state premierand lead candidate for the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), also has engagements in Magdeburg planned for Friday.

The Left Party's lead candidate Eva von Angern is appearing in Magdeburg, and the city of Halle, alongside leading party figures Heidi Reichinnek, Gregor Gysi and Dietmar Bartsch.

The Greens are planning events in Halle and Naumburg, with lead candidate Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz joined by federal party chairman Felix Banaszak.

Saxony-Anhalt's current coalition government, comprising the CDU, center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the pro-business Free Democrats (FDP),  is set to lose its majority, according to polls.

Skip next section 'Suspicious objects' found near substation in Lower Saxony: reports

'Suspicious objects' found near substation in Lower Saxony: reports

In the northwestern region of Lower Saxony, police are investigating "suspicious objects" found in the pre-dawn hours Friday morning at a power substation near the small town of Ganderkesee outside of Bremen, the Bild tabloid reported.

"A discovery was made that required a police investigation," a police spokeswoman was quoted by the newspaper as saying. A helicopter had been called in to illuminate the area from above.

No further details were immediately available.

Skip next section Police suspect another sabotage attempt near Dormagen substation

Police suspect another sabotage attempt near Dormagen substation

Police in western Germany say a suspicious device found at an electricity substation in the small city of Dormagen between Cologne and Düsseldorf was likely intended to "cause damage."

"Someone apparently tried to deliberately cause a short circuit," a Cologne police spokesperson told AFP news agency.

The object was discovered late Thursday by a passer-by. A police spokesperson said it may have been a "suspicious launching device."

The Bild tabloid reported that homemade rockets with launching devices, including timers and cooper wires, were discovered. Police have not confirmed the report.

The new discovery Friday is the latest this week in what police say are attempts at damaging critical infrastructure. 

The first incident on Tuesday near the Jänschwalde coal power plant in the eastern state of Brandenburg involved homemade projectiles resembling New Year's Eve fireworks that can short out high-voltage power lines by shooting a grounding wire over them.

A day later, similar objects were found near a power station in Bergheim, in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten morgen from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

A number of suspicious devices have been found near German power infrastructure this week, with a third incident overnight in Dormagen being treated by police as a likely sabotage attempt.

No significant damage has been reported in any of the cases and police have not revealed any suspects.

Meanwhile, parties in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt are holding their final campaign events ahead of a state election on Sunday that could see the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) come out on top.

Stay with us as we bring you the latest developments on these stories and more.

entries.title: Are data centers really bad for the planet?
entries.summary: As data centers multiply to meet AI demand, they're straining power grids, draining water supplies and reshaping the land and air around them.
entries.content:
Nature and EnvironmentGlobal issues

Are data centers really bad for the planet?

September 4, 2026

As data centers multiply to meet AI demand, they're straining power grids, draining water supplies and reshaping the land and air around them.

Every question sent to AI models provides an instant reply that seems to appear out of nowhere, but answering queries requires physical infrastructure that consumes real energy, water and land.

Somewhere around the world — maybe in Virginia, Sao Paulo or Hong Kong — a massive warehouse filled with fiber-optic cables and seemingly endless rows of humming servers is working to provide the processing power for the more than 2.5 billion questions ChatGPT alone fields daily.

AI models, along with cloud storage, streaming, web hosting and social media, all have a very real physical footprint. If data centers were a country, their level of electricity use would make them the 11th largest electricity consumer in the world, according to researchers from the United Nations University.

From energy to water to land, here's the real toll data centers take on the environment. 

An insatiable appetite for power

Data centers are becoming some of the world's fastest-growing consumers of electricity. These warehouses of servers, routers and internet-connected devices run 24/7, while cooling systems operate continuously to keep the tech from overheating. 

In Frankfurt, Germany, the grid is currently so saturated that no new connections will be available until at least the 2030s. There, data centers consume about 41% of the city's electricity. In Dublin, it's double that.

And data center electricity consumption is growing rapidly — it's expected to double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, around what Japan consumes annually, according to the International Energy Agency. 

How the AI boom could slow climate progress

All that energy has to come from somewhere, increasing reliance on fossil fuels.

One 2024 study found that more than half of the United States' data centers are powered by fossil fuels, emitting in excess of 105 million tons of CO2. Offsetting that would take more than 31,000 wind turbines running continuously for a year. 

The build-out is also keeping old coal plants alive. Utilities in the US have delayed the retirement of 15 coal-fired plants nationwide to meet surging demand, plants that together emitted nearly 65 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2023 alone.

And utilities are also constructing new gas-fired power plants, with more than 100 GW of additional facilities across the country already announced. That would lead to more carbon emissions than burning 111 million pounds (50.4 million kilograms) of coal.

Of course, data centers can also be powered by renewable energy. Pairing a facility with on-site renewables can ease pressure on the local power supply, and any surplus energy can even be sold back to the grid, making it more stable. 

However, using green electricity for data centers means there is less available for electrifying transport or decarbonizing other emissions-heavy industries.

Hidden water demand

Many data centers consume millions of gallons of water to stay cool. Servers generate constant heat, and water is one of the most effective ways to absorb and carry that heat away through evaporation.

A single large facility can use up to 5 million gallons a day, roughly the same as a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. About 80% of the water withdrawn for cooling simply evaporates; the rest becomes wastewater that can overwhelm local treatment systems never designed to handle that volume.

In northern Virginia, the almost 300 data centers clustered in one region of the US state supply about a third of the world's online traffic. There, in what is known as the world's data center capital, facilities collectively used nearly 2 billion gallons of water in 2023.

There are several more efficient ways to cool data centers. These include immersion cooling, where devices are bathed in a coolant, and closed-loop cooling systems which recycle water and can reduce freshwater use by up to 70%.

Data centers are making cities hotter

Cooling a data center doesn't get rid of the heat, it just moves it outside. That can exacerbate the urban heat island effect, which is when cities experience higher temperatures than rural areas.

Researchers in Phoenix, Arizona, found a single large data center can emit as much waste heat as tens or even hundreds of thousands of households, raising nearby land surface temperatures by up to 9 degrees Celsius (16 Fahrenheit) and air temperatures by up to 2 degrees Celsius. Those effects can be felt as far as half a kilometer away. 

Since cities are already 0.5–4 degrees Celsius warmer than their surroundings, these higher temperatures can increase heat stress risks for nearby residents and push up air conditioning demand, requiring still yet more energy.

Not all of that heat goes to waste: a growing number of data centers are capturing and piping it into nearby homes and businesses. This process, called thermal energy networks, can reduce data center power demand by up to 30%.

Coal, gas and diesel all contribute to dirty air

Powering and running data centers pollutes the air on two fronts.

First, coal and gas plants release toxic particulate matter, which can lead to respiratory disease, heart disease, asthma and more health conditions for nearby communities.

On-site diesel generators, used as backup power when the grid fails, also release harmful air pollutants. These generators pump out 200 to 600 times more nitrogen oxides than natural gas plants.

One estimate found that when backup generators for all of Virginia's data centers were emitting at just 10% of their permitted level, they could contribute to 14,000 cases of asthma symptoms, more than a dozen deaths and up to $300 million in public health costs a year.

Data centers take over large swaths of land

Data center construction requires large plots of land to build on. Repurposing natural and agricultural areas into industrial zones can threaten biodiversity and disrupt local ecosystems. 

In Hattersheim, Germany, for example, an 18-acre (7-hectare) parcel reserved for agriculture and groundwater protection — a local green space known for its rapeseed blossoms — was rezoned in 2024 to make way for a five-building data center campus.

The damage often extends beyond the site itself. Gas pipelines and power plants built to supply these facilities require their own land, fragmenting habitats and eroding soil along their routes.

Edited by: Tamsin Walker
